1. Introduction
AntarcticawassituatedinthecoreoftheGondwanasupercontinentduringthePaleozoic.Thebreakupof
GondwanaaroundAntarcticacommencedintwostages(Chenetal.,2008;König&Jokat,2006).Thefirst
was at ~167 Ma and resulted in the formation of the Mozambique Basin-Riiser-Larsen Sea between East
AntarcticaandtheAfricanPlate,andthesecondstartedat147Maandwasrelatedtoriftingbetweenthe
Antarctic Peninsula and Patagonia (König & Jokat, 2006). As a consequence of the final breakup event of
Gondwana, the Antarctic Peninsula and the South American Plate were finally separated, forming the
Drake Passage. The opening of the Drake Passage and Tasman Seaway resulted in the formation of the
AntarcticCircumpolarCurrent(ACC)(Barker,2001;Eaglesetal.,2006;Livermoreetal.,2005,2007;Munday
et al., 2015). These events were thought to result in the full glaciation of Antarctica (Barker, 2001; Barker
etal.,2007)andsignificantmodifytheglobalclimate(Barker,2001;Kennett,1977).However,therelatively
poor age constraints for the opening of the Drake Passage and the development of the ACC, from the
Eocene (Eagles, 2016a; Eagles et al., 2006; Ghiglione et al., 2008; Livermore et al., 2005; Scher & Martin,
2006)to theOligocene(Lawver& Gahagan, 2003)or theearlyMiocene (22–17 Ma) (Barker, 2001), hinder
ourunderstandingoftherelationshipbetweenglobalcoolingandoceancirculationathighlatitudes.
BasedonsimilaritiesbetweenthegeologyoftheAntarcticPeninsulaandsouthernmostAmerica,previous
studies proposed that they were once connected (e.g., Hathway, 2000; Hervé et al., 2005; Poblete et al.,
2016); however, their original spatial relationship is still debated. Several researchers have proposed that
theAntarcticPeninsulaandsouthernmostAmericawereconnectedwithalineartrend(e.g.,Dalzieletal.,
©2017.AmericanGeophysicalUnion.
AllRightsReserved. 1973; Storey, 1991; Suárez & Pettigrew, 1976), while other reconstructions place the Antarctic Peninsula
GAOETAL. 4

### page_2
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1002/2017JB014677
adjacenttothewesternpartofPatagonia(Dalzieletal.,2013;Ghidellaetal.,2002;Harrisonetal.,1979;König
&Jokat,2006;Miller,1983).WhetherthecurvedshapeofsouthernmostSouthAmericaisoriginalornotis
alsodebated.SeveralresearchershaveproposedthatthecurvedshapeofsouthernmostSouthAmericais
an original feature (Diraison et al., 2000; Eagles, 2016b; Ghiglione & Cristallini, 2007; Ramos & Aleman,
2000), while an increasing number of studies support a counterclockwise rotation of southernmost
Patagonia (Carbonell et al., 2014, 2016; Kraemer, 2003; Poblete et al., 2016), in agreement with previous
paleomagneticresults(Burnsetal.,1980;Cunninghametal.,1991;Dalzieletal.,1973).
ThereconstructionofthepaleopositionsoftheSouthAmericanPlateandtheAntarcticPeninsuladuringthe
breakupofGondwanaisbasedmainlyonmagneticanomaliesandfracturezonedatafromtheWeddellSea
andScotiaSea(Eagles,2016a;Eaglesetal.,2005;Eagles&Jokat,2014;Livermoreetal.,2005;Livermoreetal.,
2007;Lodoloetal.,2006).However,thereliabilityofthereconstructionislimitedbythelowdegreeofcer-
taintyassociatedwithmagneticisochrondata(Eagles&Jokat,2014;Ghidellaetal.,2002).
PaleomagnetismplaysanimportantroleinthetectonicreconstructionofSouthAmericaandtheAntarctic
Peninsula(Bakhmutov&Shpyra,2011;Blundell,1962;Dalzieletal.,1973;Fengetal.,1989;Grunow,1993;
Grunow et al., 1987; Kellogg, 1980; Kellogg & Reynolds, 1974, 1978; Kellogg & Rowley, 1989; Kraus et al.,
2010; Liu et al., 1991; Liu et al., 1995; Longshaw & Griffiths, 1983; Nawrocki et al., 2010; Parés & Dinarès-
Turell, 1999; Poblete et al., 2011; Valencio et al., 1979; Watts et al., 1984). For the Antarctic Peninsula, the
paleomagneticstudyofGrunow(1993)suggestedthattheAntarcticPeninsulaexperiencedclockwiserota-
tion from 175 to 155 Ma and counterclockwise rotation between 155 and 130 Ma. Other paleomagnetic
resultsfromtheAntarcticPeninsulaandtheSouthShetlandIslands(SSI)furthershowinsignificanttectonic
rotationandlatitudinaltranslationbetweentheAntarcticPeninsulaandEastAntarcticasinceabout100Ma
(e.g.,Bakhmutov&Shpyra,2011;Dalzieletal.,1973;Grunow,1993;Kellogg,1980;Kellogg&Reynolds,1978;
Krausetal.,2010;Pobleteetal.,2011;Valencioetal.,1979;Wattsetal.,1984).
Inthisstudy,wecollectedabout300paleomagneticsamplesandhandsamplesfromtheSSIforsystematic
paleomagnetic, petrographic, rock magnetic, and 40Ar/39Ar analyses and used the results to calculate the
110Maand55MapaleopolesoftheSSI.Basedonkinematicreconstructions(Bakhmutov&Shpyra,2011;
Campsetal., 2007;Grunow,1993;Kellogg&Reynolds,1978;Kellogg,1980;Nawrockietal.,2010;Poblete
etal., 2011;Prezzi etal., 2014;Poblete et al., 2016;Somoza, 2007; Somoza& Zaffarana,2008; Watts et al.,
1984)oftheAntarcticPeninsulaandSouthAmericanPlate,wediscussedtherelativemotionbetweenthe
Antarctic Peninsula and South American Plate since 110 Ma, including the opening of the Drake Passage
since~55Ma,whichmayhaveledtothedevelopmentoftheACC.
2. Geological Setting andSampling
TheAntarcticPlateincludestheWestAntarcticaandtheEastAntarcticCraton,whichareseparatedbythe
TransantarcticMountains(Chenetal.,2008;Fitzsimons,2000)(Figure1a).TheEastAntarcticCratoniscom-
posedofPrecambriantoOrdovicianmetamorphicigneousandsedimentaryrocksandwasinthecenterof
thePaleozoicsupercontinentofGondwana(Dengetal.,2014,2017;Fitzsimons,2000).EastAntarcticahas
experiencedinsignificantlatitudinalmovementsincethePaleocene(Besse&Courtillot,2002;Torsviketal.,
2012).WestAntarcticaiscomposedofatleastfourmaincrustalblocks,includingtheAntarcticPeninsula,
theThurstonIsland,theEllsworth-WhitmoreMountains,andtheMarieByrdLand(Grunow,1993)(Figure1a).
TheAntarcticPeninsulawasseparatedintothreemajordomains,includingthewestern,central,andeastern
domains,whichmayhavebeenamalgamatedduringthemid-CretaceousPalmerLandEvent(Vaughanetal.,
2012). Six lithological units can be distinguished in the Antarctic Peninsula: the metamorphic basement,
PaleozoictoTriassicsedimentaryrocks,JurassictoCenozoicsedimentaryrocks,nonmetamorphosedintrusive
rocks,JurassictoPalaeogenevolcanicrocks,andNeogenetoRecentalkalinevolcanicrocks(Burton-Johnson&
Riley,2015)(Figure1b).
TheAntarcticPeninsulavolcanicrocksweredefinedastheAntarcticPeninsulaJurassic-PaleogeneVolcanic
Group(Thomsonetal.,1983).PreviousstudiesproposedthattheAntarcticPeninsulaVolcanicGroupmay
consist of two groups (e.g., Hunter & Cantrill, 2006; Leat et al., 2009; Pankhurst et al., 2000; Riley et al.,
2001), including (i) Jurassic silicic volcanic rocks formed at the time of rifting and breakup of Gondwana
and(ii)intermediate-maficcompositionvolcanicrocksdistributedalongthewesterncoastofthepeninsula,
formed in a forearc or intra-arc environment (Riley et al., 2010). Neogene-Recent alkaline volcanic rocks

TheSSIaresituatedinthenorthwesternpartoftheAntarcticPeninsulaandhavebeenseparatedfromthe
Antarctic Peninsula by the Bransfield Strait since the Pliocene (Barker & Dalziel, 1983) (Figure 1b).
VolcanismintheSSIwaswidespreadfromtheEarlyCretaceoustothePlioceneandwasreactivatedduring
theLatePleistocene(Haaseetal.,2012).ThemigrationtrendofvolcanismisfromSWtoNEwithintheSSI
(e.g.,Haaseetal.,2012;Kraus,2005;Maestroetal.,2007;Willan&Kelley,1999).
About300coresamplesfrom40samplingsiteswerecollectedfromthesedimentaryandvolcanicrocksfrom
FildesPeninsula,KingGeorgeIsland,andByersPeninsula,LivingstonIslandoftheSSI(Table1).Allsamples
wereorientedwithamagneticcompass.ThesitelocationsweredeterminedbyGPS.Thestrikeanddipof
thevolcanicrocksweremainlymeasuredatthelithologicboundaries;measurementsweremade3–4times
tocalculateanaveragevalueateachsite.Wedidnotobserveanyobviouslocaldeviationofthemagnetic
compasswhenitwasclosetothevolcanicrocks.Declinationwascorrectedateachsitebythepresent-day
declination (D = 11.0° for Fildes Peninsula and 13.0° for Byers Peninsula), evaluated from the 12th
GenerationInternationalGeomagneticReferenceField(Thébaultetal.,2015).

aroundPreciousPeakandUllmannSpuroftheKellerPeninsula,AdmiraltyBay,KingGeorgeIsland.Later,
Barton (1965) proposed that the volcanic rocks in the south Fildes Peninsula formed in the Jurassic with
their age constrained by the strong petrological affinities with the Upper Jurassic volcanic rocks of the
Antarctic Peninsula. Barton (1965) assigned other rocks in the peninsula to the Fildes Peninsula Group,
with a middle Tertiary age, constrained by plant fossils and stratigraphic correlation. Hawkes (1961)
ascribed the Fildes Peninsula Group to the early Miocene, constrained by stratigraphic correlation, while
Adie (1964) assigned the Group to the late Oligocene. Smellie et al. (1984) changed the Fildes Peninsula
Group to the Fildes Peninsula Formation and divided it into three members: a lower member of coarse
porphyriticbasaltandbasalticandesitelavasinterbeddedwithlaterallydiscontinuousvolcaniclasticrocks,
a middle member of volcaniclastic rocks with a few basalt and basaltic andesite lavas, and an upper
memberwithfine-grainedaphyricandmicroporphyriticandesiteanddacitelavas.Thelowestmemberin
the southern peninsula was dated to circa 58 Ma by the K-Ar whole-rock method, while the basaltic
andesite from the lower member of the northern peninsula had a younger K-Ar age of 48–58 Ma; in
addition,theageoftheandesiticrocksoftheuppermemberwasconstrainedto42–46MausingtheK-Ar
method (Smellie et al., 1984). Machado (1997) separated the Fildes Peninsula group into four formations,
from bottom to top: Clement Hill (basalts, basaltic andesites, and andesites interbedded with polymictic

Figure5.SimplifiedgeologicalmapofByersPeninsula,LivingstonIsland,SSI,WestAntarctica(modifiedfromHathwayetal.,1998;seeFigure1forthelocation).
Berriasian-Valanginian Mixed Marine, Agglomerate, and Lower Cretaceous Volcanic. Crame et al. (1993)
changed the Byers Peninsula succession to group status and divided the strata previously designated as
Mudstone and Mixed Marine members into four formations: Anchorage, Devils Point, President Beaches,
and Chester Cone. Hathway and Lomas (1998) revised and extended the lithostratigraphic scheme
proposed by Crame et al. (1993) and Hathway (1997) and separated the group into five formations:
Anchorage(?Kimmeridgian-Tithonian),PresidentBeaches(Berriansian),Start Hill(lateBerriansian),Chester
Cone (?latest Berriasian-mid Valanginian), and Cerro Negro (early Aptian) (Figure 5). New 40Ar/39Ar ages
from the base (120.3 ± 2.2 Ma on silicic pyroclasti plagioclase) and topmost (119 ± 3.0 Ma on ignimbrite
plagioclase) parts of the Cerro Negro formation confirm that the formation was deposited in the early
Aptiantimes(Hathwayetal.,1999).
In this study, the Sealer Hill columnar basalts were sampled from one site (nine samples; BP1 in Table 1)
(Figures1,5,and6a);K-Arand40Ar/39Ardatingindicatedagesof108±4.0Ma(Pankhurstetal.,1979)and
111Ma(Wattsetal.,1984),respectively.ColumnarbasaltsatVietorRockwerealsosampledatthreesites
(27 samples; BP2-4 in Table 1) (Figures 5 and 6b); the 40Ar/39Ar age of the basalt is 104 Ma (Watts et al.,
1984), and the K-Ar whole-rock age is 107 ± 4.0 Ma (Pankhurst et al., 1979). Volcaniclastic rocks of the
CerroNegroFormationweresampledatonesite(10samples;BP5inTable1)(Figures5and6c).

3. 40Ar/39ArAnalyses oftheFildes Peninsula Basalt Samples
3.1. SamplingandMethodology
Wecollectedbasaltsamplesfor40Ar/39ArincrementalheatinganalysesfromthetoppartoftheJasperHill
Formation(samplingsiteinFigures2,7a,and7bandTable2),thetoppartoftheAgateBeachFormation
(samplingsiteinFigures2,7c,and7dandTable2),themiddletoppartoftheBlockHillFormation(sampling
site in Figures 2, 7e, and 7f and Table 2), and the top part of the Long Hill Formation (sampling site in
Figures2,7g,and7handTable2).TheaimwastoconfirmtheaccuracyofpreviousK-Ardatesand/orto
reducetheuncertaintyoftheageconstraints.Thinsectionanalysesrevealedthatthemainmineralsinthe
basaltsamplesarepyroxene,plagioclase,hornblende,biotite,andmagnetite.
ThesamplepreparationprocedurefollowedDuncanandKeller(2004).Theseparatedgroundmassfraction
samples were placed in evacuated quartz tubes, wrapped in Cu foil alternating with packages of Fish
Canyon Tuff sanidine flux monitors provided by the New Mexico Tech laboratory (FCT-NM) standard
(28.201±0.023Ma;Kuiperetal.,2008),andirradiatedfor6hintheOregonStateUniversityTRIGAreactor
in-coreirradiationtube(ICIT)facility.Parabolicinterpolationwasusedtocalculatethevaluesoftheirradiation
parameterJ.EstimateduncertaintiesforJare0.2–0.3%standarddeviation(Koppersetal.,2000).Corrections
ofKandCarelatedtointerferingreactionsaregiveninWijbransetal.(1995)(Koppersetal.,2000).
40Ar/39Arresultsweredeterminedwithincrementalheating,carriedoutoncrystalline300–600μmground-
masssampleswithacontinuous10WCO laserprobeconnectedwithaMAP–215/50massspectrometer,at
2
OregonStateUniversity(Aydin,2014).WeusedtheArArCALCv2.2softwaretocalculatetheincrementalheat-
ing plateau and isochron ages (Koppers, 2002). The 1σ level errors for the 40Ar/39Ar ages are presented.
Typically,32–33heatingstepsforeachgroundmasssamplewereperformedtoproduceplateauages,com-
posed of 5–12 steps (Figure 7 and Table 2). We interpret the plateau ages as reliable crystallization ages,
whichareequivalenttotheisochronages(Duncan&Al–Amri,2013).
3.2. Results
New40Ar/39ArplateauagesforthetoppartoftheJasperHillFormation,thetoppartoftheAgateBeach
Formation,themiddletoppartoftheBlockHillFormation,andthetoppartoftheLongHillFormationare
asfollows:55.09±0.25Ma,56.38±0.20Ma,54.66±0.56Ma,and52.42±0.19Ma,respectively(Figure7).
Sincetheinverseisochronageishighlyconsistentwiththeplateauage,weusetheplateauagetorepresent
theeruptionage.
4. Petrography
Toidentifythemagneticcarriers,fiverepresentativespecimensfromtheFossilHillFormation(volcaniclastic
rock;FH4-1,FH2-1),BlockHillFormation(basalt,BH5-3)ofFildesPeninsula,SealerHill(basalt,BP1-1),Vietor
Rock(basalt,BP2-6),andCerroNegroFormation(volcaniclasticrocks,BP5-1)ofByersPeninsulawerestudied
usingapetrographicmicroscope(Figure8).ThreerepresentativespecimensfromtheJasperHillFormation
(basalt,JH1-3),BlockHillFormation(basalt,BH5-3),andLongHillFormation(basaltLH6-1)werestudiedusing
aZeissSUPPA55fieldemissionscanningelectronmicroscope(FESEM)under10kVacceleratingvoltagewith
a working distanceof 3–9 mm(Figure 9). The microzoneelemental composition wasanalyzed by energy
dispersiveX-rayspectrometer(EDS)(Figure9)atChinaUniversityofGeosciences,Beijing.

4.1. Results
Microscopic observations indicate that the specimens from Fildes Peninsula have undergone extensive
chloritization (Figures 8a and 8b), sericitization (Figures 8c and 8d), and chalcopyrite mineralization
(Figure 8e). Ti-free magnetite and oxidized (cation deficient) titanomagnetite are identified as the main
magneticcarriersfromFESEMandEDSstudies(Figures9a,9b,9d,9e,9g,and9h).
Ti-freemagnetiteismainlyformedbyahighdegreeoflow-temperaturealterationoftitanomagnetite(Van
der Voo et al., 1993). These pure magnetites were observed growing with chalcopyrite and chalcocite
(Figures 9a and 9b) and along the borders of mafic minerals (Figures 9a–9h), further confirming its
low-temperaturefluidorigin(VanderVooetal.,1993).Mostofthetitanomagnetitehasexperiencedlow-
temperatureoxidationalterationandhasacharacteristicbrightgrayishcolorandextensiveirregular,curved
shrinkagecracksunderreflectedlightmicroscopyandFESEM(Figures9i–9l)(Petersen&Vali,1987).Thesmall
grainsize(<20μm)ofthecationdeficienttitanomagnetiteandtheTi-freemagnetiteraisesthepossibilityof
their carrying a secondary magnetization (Johnson & Merrill, 1973; Nishitani & Kono, 1989; Van der Voo
etal.,1993).
Figure8.Microphotographsofremagnetizedspecimensfrom(a–d)FildesPeninsula,KingGeorgeIsland,and(e–h)ByersPeninsula,LivingstonIsland.Transmitted
lightandreflectedlightmicroscopyphotographsindicatingextensivechloritization(Figures8aand8b)andsericitization(Figure8c)inthespecimens.Reflected
lightphotographsshowingthatmagnetite(Figures8b–8h)isthemainmagneticcarrier,growingalongtherimofthealteredmineralsandwithchalcopyrite,
confirmingthesecondaryoriginofthemagnetite.Themagnetitegrowingwithintheplagioclasemaycarryaprimarymagnetization(Figures8fand8g).Chl:chlorite,
Mag:magnetite,Pl:plagioclase,andCcp:chalcopyrite.

### page_12

Figure9.Fieldemissionscanningelectronmicroscope(FESEM)imagesandenergydispersiveX-rayspectrometer(EDS)pointanalysisofTi-freemagnetite,Ti-mag-

Unlike the widespread chloritization and sericitization within lavas of Fildes Peninsula, most of the mafic
minerals from the intrusive rocks of Byers Peninsula are not influenced by hydrothermal alteration
(Figures 8f and 8g). Therefore, the fine-grained (<20 μm) titanomagnetite growing within the unaltered
maficmineralswaswellisolatedfromhydrothermalalterationbytheprotectionofthemaficminerals,and
thus, it may record the primary magnetization (Figures 8f and 8g) (Astudillo et al., 2010; Feinberg et al.,
2005;Pobleteetal.,2011;Renneetal.,2002).ThevolcaniclasticrocksfromtheCerroNegroFormationwere
strongly altered, revealed by the occurrence of secondary magnetite, which may carry a
remagnetizationdirection.

IRMacquisitioncurvesweremeasured,andthermaldemagnetizationofthreeorthogonalIRMcomponents
(Lowrie, 1990) was conducted to further evaluate the magnetic mineralogy. The orthogonal IRMs were

Hysteresis loops and FORCs were measured by using an alternating gradient magnetometer (MicroMag

methodwasusedtodistinguishbetweentheprimarythermoremanent(TRM)andsecondarychemicalrema-
nent(CRM)magnetizationsofrepresentativespecimens(Ali&Aitchison,2002;Cisowskietal.,1990;Fuller

spectraofbothNRMandIRM,usingequivalentfields.
5.2. Results
Progressive acquisition of IRM revealed that the magnetizations of the samples were saturated below
~200mT(Figures10a1–10a4),confirmingthepresenceoflow-coercivityphases.Twomineralswereidenti-
fiedwithunblockingtemperatureat~580°Candabove600°Cbythermaldemagnetizationofthreeorthogo-
nalIRMcomponentsfromspecimensofFildesPeninsula:thefirstwithlowcoercivity,andwhichmaybepure
magnetite, and the second is most likely cation-deficient titanomagnetite (Sherwood & Mallik, 1996)
(Figures 10b1–10b3). Specimens from Byers Peninsula also have a low coercivity and a high unblocking
temperatureof~590°C,indicatingmagnetite.
Closedhysteresisloopsbelow200mTindicatethepredominanceofalow-coercivitycomponent(Figure11).
MostoftheFORCdiagramsexhibitadivergingcontourpatternindicativeofmultidomain(MD)grains(Pike
etal.,2001;Qinetal.,2008)(Figure11).ThelessdivergentcontourpatterninFH4–4,andtheHcvalueof
~20mTatthepeakofthedistribution,indicatethepresenceofsingledomain(SD)magnetite(Dunlop&
Özdemir,2001;Muxworthy&Dunlop,2002;Robertsetal.,2000).

7. Discussion
7.1. Reliabilityofthe40Ar/39ArResults
Basedon23K-AragesobtainedduringChina’sfirst,second, andthirdscientificexpeditionstoAntarctica
(1985–1988)and30publishedK-Arages(Smellieetal.,1984),theageoftheJasperHillandAgateBeach
FormationfromtheFildesPeninsulais 54.3±0.6–64.4±0.8Ma,andtheageoftheFossil HillFormation,
Block Hill Formation, and Long Hill Formation is 42 ± 1.0–54.18 ± 0.94 Ma (Li et al., 1992; Li & Liu, 1987)
(Figure3).Zhuetal.(1991)furtherassignedtheJasperHillFormationtothelatePaleocenebasedonRb-Sr
(54Ma)and40Ar/39Ar(55Ma)dating.TheageoftheAgateBeachFormationis45–50MabasedonK-Ardat-
ing;theageoftheFossilHillFormationisOligocene-Eocene;andtheageoftheBlockHillFormationismiddle
Miocene(Figure3).Inaddition,Haaseetal.(2012)reportedthree40Ar-39Ar/K-Ardatafromthenorthernpart
of the Fildes Peninsula and the eastern part of Nelson Island, which are 56.1 ± 0.3, 55.21 ± 0.49, and
55.8 ± 1.0 Ma. The age from the Jasper Hill to Long Hill Formation in this study is Late Paleocene-early
Eocene,whichisdifferentfromearlydivisionbytheK-Armethod(Lietal.,1992;Li&Liu,1987;Zhuetal.,
1991)(Figure3).
Mostsecondaryminerals,suchasTi-freemagnetite,growaroundthegroundmassmineralsandcanbeeasily
removedbypreliminarytreatments.However,someofthesecondaryminerals,suchassericiteandchlorite,
arenoteasilyremovedbywet-chemicalcleaningmethodswhentheyaregrowingwithinthegroundmass
minerals;therefore,theymayaffectthedating.However,inourstudy,theargondataexhibitawell-defined
ageplateauathigh-temperaturesteps(Figure7),suggestingthatsecondarymineralsarenotthedominant
phaseinthemineralcoresandhaveaminorinfluenceonthedatingresults(Wangetal.,2009).Mostimpor-
tantly,ourresultsdonothaveanexcessArcomponent,asshownbyinitial(40Ar/36Ar) ratiosof295.20±24.8 0
(AB1,AgateBeachFormation),297.42 ±1.3(BH5,BlockHillFormation),and295.18 ±24.5(LH6,LongHill
Formation)(Table2).Theinitial(40Ar/36Ar) ratio(255.39±138.68)ofbasaltfromtheJasperHillFormation
0
(JH1) is too low, meaning that these samples may have experienced stronger secondary alteration.

Moreover,theformationageoftheAgateBeachFormation(56.38±0.25Ma)isolderthantheJasperHill
Formation(55.09 ±0.25 Ma),whichis inconsistent with thefact that theJasper HillFormation is covered
by the Agate Beach Formation (Li et al., 1996). Therefore, the 40Ar/36Ar age for the Jasper Hill Formation
from this study cannot be used to constrain the age of this formation. In conclusion, the age of the
sampledFildesPeninsularocksisfrom52.42±0.19Mato56.38±0.20Ma.
7.2. RemagnetizationinFildesPeninsula
NRM/IRMdemagnetizationplotssuggestthatthespecimenshaveexperiencedaremagnetizationeventand
acquiredasecondarychemicalremanentmagnetization(CRM)(Figure12).Thisissupportedbythepresence
ofpuremagnetiteandcationdeficienttitanomagnetiteofsecondaryorigin,whichhavetheabilitytocarry
secondaryremagnetizationdirection(Figures8and9).Ournewwhole-rock40Ar/36Arplateauageshowsthat
theAgate Beach Formation formed during a reversed polarity interval (chron C24r) (Vandenberghe et al.,
2012);however,thepaleomagneticdataindicatethatthespecimenshaveanormalpolarity,whichconfirms
thattheywereremagnetized.Inaddition,theFossilHillFormationunconformablyoverliestheAgateBeach
FormationandisconformablyoverlainbytheBlockHillFormation.Basedonournewwhole-rock40Ar/39Ar
plateauageconstraints,theFossilHillFormationwasdepositedbetween56.38±0.2and54.66±0.56Ma,dur-
inga reversedpolarity interval which wecorrelated to chron C24r (Vandenbergheet al., 2012) (Figure 3).
However, the paleomagnetic results indicate a normal polarity for the Fossil Hill Formation (Figure 13d),
andtherefore,weconcludethatthesedimentaryrocksoftheFossilHillFormationwerealsoremagnetized.
ThelavasandvolcaniclasticrocksfromtheAgateBeachformationandFossilHillFormationwerecutthrough
byverticalintrusivebasaltdikes(sitename:FHD).Ourdatashowthatboththelavasandintrusiverockshave
normalpolarity(Figure13jandTable1).Inaddition,theBlockHillFormationandLongHillFormationarecut

throughbyverticalintrusivebasaltdikes(sitename:LHD),andtheyhavethesamedirectionandreversed
polarity (Figure 13j and Table 1). Therefore, we deduce that the lavas were remagnetized from intrusive
eventsrelatedtolow-temperaturefluidsandrecordedantipodalmagnetizations.
Although direct isotopic ages of these intrusive rocks are still unknown, previous studies have provided
considerable information about the remagnetization age of these lava flows. It is interesting to note that
there is a series of magmatic dikes widely distributed in King George Island. Kraus (2005) conducted a
systematicAr-Aragestudyof thedikesinFildesPeninsulaofKingGeorgeIslandandgavetheformation
age of dikes ranged from the Thanetian to Ypresian with an average age of 55 Ma. The dike ages are
similar to the reported ages in the lava flows of this study, suggesting a genetic relation between dikes
and lava flows. Taking this into account and the difficulty to measure the bedding in irregular lava flows
astheoneinFildesPeninsula,itispossiblethatthealterationinthelavaflowsoccurredduringorslightly
after its deposition. Thus, we propose that the volcanic rocks in Fildes Peninsula were remagnetized at
about 55 Ma.
The negative reversal test may be caused by the errors in sample orientation, incomplete demagnetiza-
tion, inadequate sampling of paleosecular variation (PSV) during either (or both) of the polarity intervals,
thenondipolemagneticfields,asymmetricreversalsnatureintheearlyEocene,aregionalrelativetectonic
movementamongthesamplingsites,ortheremagnetizationevents(e.g.,Butler,1998;Liuetal.,2012;Van
der Voo et al., 1993). In this study, the errors in sample orientation, incomplete demagnetization,
nondipole magnetic fields, or asymmetric reversals nature in the early Eocene and regional relative
tectonicmovementamongthesamplingsitescanbeeasilyruledout.Theremagnetizationeventoccurred
within a small time span, during which the Antarctic Peninsula cannot experience significant tectonic
movement(e.g.,Grunow,1993;Pobleteetal.,2011;Wattsetal.,1984).Theabnormalpaleolatitudescalcu-
latedfromthenormal((cid:1)72.8°S)andreversal((cid:1)55.4°S)polaritydataindicatethatthenegativereversaltest
is most likely caused by the inadequate sampling of PSV during both of the polarity intervals.
7.3. MagnetizationinByersPeninsula
The Sealer Hill and Vietor Rock lava flows overlain the volcaniclastic rocks of the Cerro Negro Formation
(112–125Ma)(Figure5).Thenegligibledipangle(~4°)ofthesevolcaniclasticrocks(Figures5and6c)indi-
catesthatthe~20°tiltofthelavaflowsisalocale,butoriginalorientation,whichmightrelatetoirregular
topography (Figures 6a and 6b) and has not used for tilt corrections both in a previous study (Grunow,
1993)andinthisstudy.
NRM/IRMdemagnetizationplotsshowthatthebasaltspecimensmostlikelyrecordaTRM(Figure12),indi-
catingthatthesespecimensmayretainaprimarymagnetization.Themicroscopicobservationsfurtherprove
that this primary magnetization is mainly recorded by fine-grained silicate-hosted magnetite (Figures 8f
and8g).
Takinginto accounttheabove analyses,theoverlappingof thesite meandirections of samples fromthe
Fildes Peninsula and the Byers Peninsula with the geocentric axial dipole (GAD) field (Dec = 360.0° and
Inc=(cid:1)75.2°fortheFildesPeninsulaandDec=360.0°andInc=(cid:1)75.5°fortheByersPeninsula)ismostlikely
a result of insignificant tectonic movement of these peninsulas since about 110 Ma (e.g., Grunow, 1993;
Pobleteetal.,2011;Wattsetal.,1984)(Figures13jand14c).

7.6. OroclinalBendingoftheAntarcticPeninsula
WhethertheAntarcticPeninsulaunderwentoroclinalbendingisstilldebated,andpaleomagneticdataplay
animportantroleinmeasuringlarge-scaledeformationorlatitudinaltranslationofthecrust.Hamilton(1966)
concludedthatthepaleomagneticresultsofBlundell(1962)revealedsignificantstructuraldistortionofthe
northernpartofthepeninsulaaftertheCretaceous.However,fromadditionaldatafromtheLassiterCoast
intrusion (~90–120 Ma, summarized by Vaughan et al., 2012), from the southern part of the peninsula,
togetherwithdatafromnorthernpartofthepeninsulaofBlundell(1962)andDalzieletal.(1973),Kellogg
andReynolds(1978)supportedtheconclusionsofDalzieletal.(1973)thatnosignificantpost-Cretaceous
tectonicbendingofthenorthernpeninsulaoccurred.Inaddition,theysuggestedthatthesouthernOrville
CoastandEasternEllsworthLandexperienced~50°clockwiserotationsincetheEarlyCretaceouscompared
withthenorthernpartofthepeninsula(Kellogg,1980;Kellogg&Rowley,1989).KelloggandRowley(1989)
alsoproposedthattheoroclinalbendformedaftertheLateCretaceous.However,Wattsetal.(1984)and
Grunow(1993)supportedtheideaofapparentpolarwanderofthestablepartoftheAntarcticPeninsula
inthemid-Cretaceous,ratherthanregionaloroclinalbendingof thenorthernpeninsulacomparedto the
stableAntarcticPeninsula.
From a comparison of our new calculated paleopole of 110 Ma for the northern part of the Antarctic
Peninsula with the paleopoles from Orville Coast and Eastern Ellsworth Land and Thurston Island, we
conclude that the Orville Coast, Eastern Ellsworth Land, and Thurston Island have experienced clockwise
rotation (33.0 ± 27.9° and 35.7 ± 24.7°) after ~110 Ma compared to the northern part of the Antarctic
Peninsula(BPandPS)(Figure16andTableS3).
Previousreportedgeologicalevidencesmayprovidesomeexplanationsforthestructuraldistortionbetween
thenorthernandsouthernpartoftheAntarcticPeninsulaandThurstonIsland.Fromstructuralandisotopic

chronologyconstraintsfromPalmerLand,inadditiontoLassiterCoast,OrvilleCoast,andEasternEllsworth

at ~107 Ma, with the main compressional direction of 341°, and the other at ~103 Ma, with the main
compressional direction of 259.5°. Vaughan et al. (2012) further proposed that the overlap of these two
compressional events caused the oroclinal bending of the peninsula, which is consistent with our
interpretationofthepaleomagneticdata.Thus,ournewdatasupporttheideathattheoroclinalbending
oftheAntarcticPeninsulawascausedbythePalmerLandEvent;however,consideringthesmallnumber

paleomagnetic data, we suggest that more paleomagnetic and isotopic chronology researches in Palmer
Landareneededtobetterunderstandtheformationprocessandgeodynamicbackgroundoftheoroclinal
bendingofthePeninsula.
7.7. PlateReconstructionoftheAntarcticPeninsulaandSouthAmericaSince110Ma
A series of tectonic and magmatic events have occurred in the Antarctic Peninsula since the Middle
Cretaceous.InthenorthernpartoftheAntarcticPeninsula,accompaniedbythesubductionofoceaniccrust
ofthePhoenixPlate,asignificantvolcaniccalc-alkalinebeltdevelopedfromtheCretaceoustotheCenozoic
(González-Ferrán, 1985). In the southern Antarctic Peninsula, the mid-Cretaceous Palmer Land Event has
beenidentified,withtwointervals(at~107Maand103Ma)ofcompressioninPalmerLand(Vaughanetal.,
2012;Vaughan&Storey,2000).However,thetectonicmovementoftheAntarcticPeninsula,aswellasthe
possibilityofrelativemovementamongtheAntarcticPeninsula,SouthAmerica,andEastAntarcticaduring
oceaniccrustsubduction,remainsunclear.
PreviousplatereconstructionsofSouthAmericaandtheAntarcticPeninsulaarebasedmainlyonseafloor
magneticanomalies,fracturezonedata,andpaleomagnetism;forexample,Ghidellaetal.(2002)deduced
that the Antarctic Peninsula moved southward relative to South America after the breakup of Gondwana
and then experienced clockwise rotation to the present position after 90 Ma (Cunningham et al., 1995;
Ghidella et al., 2002). Poblete et al. (2016) reconstructed the paleopositions of South America and the
Antarctic Peninsula since 120 Ma and proposed the oroclinal bending of southernmost Patagonia
(Figure 17a) since the mid-Cretaceous. Paleomagnetic data show a continuous counterclockwise rotation
ofsouthernmostPatagoniasincethemid-Cretaceous(Figure17b),supportingtherigidlithosphericblocks
rotationmodel(Pobleteetal.,2014,2016;Rapalinietal.,2016),inagreementwithstructuralandanalogmod-
elsinTierradelFuego(Figure17a)(Carbonelletal.,2014,2016;Kraemer,2003).However,basedonthenew
EulerrotationsfromseafloorspreadingdataintheWeddellSea,Eagles(2016b)locatedapolefortheclosure
oftheRocasVerdesBasininequatoriallatitudesatmid-Cretaceous(Figure17a),whichprecludesthepossi-
bility of plate rotations proposed by Poblete et al. (2016) and favors a model of regional strike-slip faults
movement causing crustal rotation and deformation. Clearly, a dynamic tectonic reconstruction between
SouthAmericaandtheAntarcticPeninsulaisthekeytoresolvingthesedisputes.
Basedonananalysisofmarinegeophysicaldata,Livermoreetal.(2005)proposedthattheshallow(<1,000m
depth)gatewaywasformedduringthemiddleEocenewith57kmofN-SseparationbetweentheAntarctic
PeninsulaandSouthAmerica,followedby278kmofWNW-ESEextensionbetween50and33Ma,andadeep
waterexchangesince34–30Ma(Figure17a).Ontheotherhand,fieldandgeophysicaldatafromTierradel
FuegoinSouthAmerica,andProtectorBasinandDoveBasinintheAntarcticPeninsula(Figure17a),supporta
latestPaleocene-earlyEoceneextensionbetweenSouthAmericaandtheAntarcticPeninsula(Eaglesetal.,
2006; Ghiglione et al., 2008). The extension in these regions supports an early phase shallow-depth or
intermediate-depthoceaniccirculationbetweenthePacificandAtlanticOceans(Eaglesetal.,2006).Inaddi-
tion,theEocene-OligoceneabyssalenvironmentsintheTierradelFuegoandtheNorthScotiaRidgehave
beenreconstructedfromacompilationofstratigraphicrecords(Figure17a),andtheyconfirmtheearlyopen-
ingoftheDrakePassage(Lagabrielleetal.,2009).LawverandGahagan(2003)alsoproposedanearlyforma-
tion of the Drake Passage at 31 ± 2.0 Ma, which is supported by the occurrence of profound
paleoceanographic and paleoproductivity changes in the Southern Ocean (Diester-Haass & Zahn, 1996;
Kennett&Stott,1990).
We combined the previous South America middle Cretaceous (125–100 Ma) (Somoza & Zaffarana, 2008),
Late Cretaceous-Paleocene (85–65 Ma) (Somoza & Zaffarana, 2008), and Eocene (50–40 Ma) (Somoza,
2007) results with our new calculated 110 Ma and 55 Ma paleopoles, and the 90 Ma paleopole from

Poblete et al. (2011) for the Antarctic Peninsula, to reconstruct the paleopositions of South America and
theAntarctic Peninsula from theEarly Cretaceous to the early Eocene (Figure 17a and Table S3). Wealso
reconstructedtheAntarcticPeninsulapaleopositionat27Mausinga27MapaleopolefromtheKerguelen
Islands (Antarctic Plate) (Camps et al., 2007) (Table S3) and attempted to reconstruct the opening of the
Drake Passage since the early Eocene.
Theconsistencyofthepositionofthe110MapaleopolesfromByersPeninsula,LivingstonIsland,SSIand
Penola Strait, and the Antarctic Peninsula, as well as the 110 Ma reference pole from the East Antarctica
apparentpolarwanderpath(Besse&Courtillot,2002;Torsviketal.,2012),supportsthepreviousproposed
insignificant relative tectonic rotation among the SSI, Antarctic Peninsula, and the East Antarctica since
110Ma(e.g.,Grunow,1993;Pobleteetal.,2011)(Figure16andTableS3).Ourplatereconstructionsshowthat
the Antarctic Peninsula and South America were connected at 110 Ma, and they experienced southward
movementandclockwiserotationfrom110Mato27Ma(Figure17b).Theoroclinalbendingofsouthernmost
SouthAmericawasreconstructedfrom110Mato55MafromthereconstructionofPobleteetal.(2016)and
revealsacontinuouscounterclockwiserotationofsouthernmostPatagonia(Figure17b).Theangulardevia-
tionforthe45MapaleopoleofbothSouthAmericaandtheAntarcticPeninsulaisconsistentwiththe90Ma
paleomagneticpoleoftheseplatesfromPobleteetal.(2011)(Figure17b).
PaleomagneticdatacanbeusedtoconstrainthewidthoftheDrakePassage.Inourstudy,thepaleomagnetic
data indicate that the Antarctic Peninsula and South America were still connected at 55 Ma (Figure 17b),
meaningthattheDrakePassagehadnotyetformed.Thereconstructionsuggestsasouthwardmovement
and clockwise rotation of the Antarctic Peninsula from 55 to 27 Ma, resulting in the separation of South
AmericaandtheAntarcticPeninsula.Thisrapidseparationissupportedbypreviousresearch;forexample,
Cunningham et al. (1995) suggested that the north-south divergence rate between southernmost South
AmericaandthenortherntipoftheAntarcticPeninsulawashighestinthe40–20Matimeinterval.Finally,
the modern Drake Passage formed after the northward translation of the South America since 27 Ma
(Figure17).

8. Conclusions
1. StableHTCscarriedbysecondaryTi-freemagnetiteandcationdeficienttitanomagnetitewereisolated
fromvolcanicandsedimentaryrocks fromFildesPeninsula,KingGeorgeIsland,SSI. Theygivethesite
meandirectionofD =193.2°(±18.6°),I =75.5°(±4.7°),k =59.2,andα =4.7°beforetiltcorrection.
g g g 95
Combining thelow NRM/IRMratios, inconsistency with the polarityconstrained by thepaleomagnetic
results,and40Ar/39Arplateauageconstraints,weproposethatthespecimensfromFildesPeninsulawere
remagnetizedduringthemagmaticeventat~55Ma.
2. LavasfromtheByersPeninsula,KingGeorgeIsland,SSI,carryaprimarythermoremanentmagnetization.
TheygivethesitemeandirectionofDg=344.9°(±26.4°),Ig=(cid:1)70.3°(±8.9°),kg=106.9,andα =8.9°.
95
3. PaleomagneticdatashowthattheOrvilleCoast,EasternEllsworthLand,andThurstonIslandhaveexperi-
encedclockwiserotationcomparedtothenorthernpartoftheAntarcticPeninsula(ByersPeninsulaand
PenolaStrait).ThisdifferentialcrustaltectonicrotationmayreflecttheinfluenceofthePalmerLandEvent
duringthemid-Cretaceous.
4. The new paleopoles for the Antarctic Peninsula and SSI show that the Antarctic Peninsula and South
America were connected and experienced a southward movement and clockwise rotation during
110–55Ma.SouthwardtranslationandclockwiserotationoftheAntarcticPeninsulaledtotheseparation
oftheAntarcticPeninsulaandSouthAmericafrom55to27Ma.Subsequently,thenorthwardtranslation
ofSouthAmericaafter27MafurtherincreasedtheN-SdivergencebetweentheAntarcticPeninsulaand
SouthAmerica,finallyformingthemodernDrakePassage.
